title: Loved by Jonathan, Feared by Saul
summary: After the victory over Goliath, Jonathan binds himself to David in a covenant of love and gives him his robe and weapons. David succeeds in every mission, and the women's song crediting him with tens of thousands turns Saul's admiration into jealousy. Saul twice tries to spear him, sends him into danger, and offers his daughters in marriage hoping the Philistines will kill him, but David succeeds, marries Michal, and Saul becomes his lasting enemy.
story: Chapter 17 made David a national hero. Chapter 18 shows what that fame does to the people around him. Almost everyone loves David: Jonathan, Michal, all Israel and Judah, even Saul's servants. Saul alone fears him, and his fear grows at every step. The chapter repeats that the LORD was with David and had departed from Saul, which explains both David's success and Saul's dread. Jonathan's covenant, begun here, will shape David's story long after Jonathan's death (2 Samuel 9). Michal's love and marriage bring David into the royal family, which gives him a claim on the throne and also a place inside Saul's reach.
historical:
The chapter continues in the court at Gibeah, Saul's hometown in Benjamin, which served as his royal base. Saul's court was small by later standards: a household, a few officers, a commander (Abner), and troops raised from the tribes. David's rise from court musician to army commander and royal son-in-law happens within this modest setting, and it shows how quickly a gifted warrior could become a political rival. Merab's marriage to Adriel of Meholah (verse 19) is mentioned again in 2 Samuel 21:8, where her sons are handed over to the Gibeonites.

The chapter's text has a history of its own. The oldest Greek manuscripts are shorter here, as they are in chapter 17, and lack several passages, including the account of Saul's offer of Merab. Scholars disagree about whether the longer Hebrew text or the shorter Greek text is closer to the earliest form of the story. The overall shape of events is the same in both.
cultural:
Jonathan's gift of his robe, tunic, sword, bow, and belt was more than generosity. Clothing and weapons could represent a person's identity and position, and the crown prince's robe on David's shoulders is a striking picture of Jonathan handing over what would have been his. Covenant in this setting means a binding, sworn commitment between two parties, often with obligations extending to their families. The word "love" was also used in political alliances in the ancient Near East to describe loyalty between allies, and that sense sits alongside the personal affection in this chapter.

Victory songs by women, with dancing and tambourines, were a traditional way to welcome returning warriors (compare Miriam in Exodus 15:20-21 and Jephthah's daughter in Judges 11:34). The song's pairing of "thousands" with "tens of thousands" is a normal pattern of Hebrew poetry, which rises from one number to a larger one for emphasis, but Saul hears it as a ranking. A bride-price (mohar) was paid by the groom to the bride's family (Exodus 22:16-17). David, as a poor man, could not pay a royal one, and Saul turns the custom into a trap by demanding proof of a hundred dead Philistines.
literary: The chapter is built on the repetition of two short statements: the LORD was with David, and Saul was afraid. Saul's fear intensifies in stages (verses 12, 15, and 29), while David's success is repeated (verses 5, 14, 15, and 30). The verb "love" also recurs: Jonathan loves David, all Israel and Judah love him, Michal loves him, and even Saul's servants are said to love him. Saul is the only figure whose inner thoughts are reported, and they are schemes. The narrator lets the reader see Saul's plans ("let the hand of the Philistines be against him") while David, in his replies, speaks only of his own unworthiness. The Hebrew verb for David's success (sakal, to act wisely and prosper) sounds almost like the verb Samuel used when he said Saul had acted foolishly in 13:13, a contrast audible in Hebrew.

outline.t: Jonathan's covenant with David; David's success
The women's song and Saul's jealousy
Saul's spear, and the LORD with David
Merab promised and given to another
Michal's love and the price of a hundred Philistines

doctrines.note: Each of Saul's schemes to get rid of David ends by advancing him: command of troops makes him loved, the Philistine test makes him a son-in-law. God's purposes move forward through the very plans meant to stop them.

Jonathan's covenant with David is a human bond sworn before God, with lasting obligations to both families. It gives the Old Testament one of its fullest pictures of covenant loyalty between persons, which later shapes David's kindness to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth.
Saul's jealousy begins with a song and grows into fear, scheming, and murderous intent. The chapter traces how envy of another's blessing can take over a life that has turned from God.

words.note: Ahav, to love. It is used of Jonathan, Michal, the people, and Saul's servants. The word covers deep personal affection and also, in covenant and political settings, loyal commitment. Here both senses are present in Jonathan's love.

Berit, covenant, a solemn and binding agreement. Jonathan and David's covenant is renewed in 20:8-17 and 23:18, and David honors it after Jonathan's death. The word is the same used for God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, and Israel.

Sakal, to act wisely, to prosper. It describes David's success (verses 5, 14, 15, and 30), a success that combines skill with God's blessing. The idea is not luck but effective wisdom that comes from the LORD being with him.

Mohar, bride-price, the payment from a groom to a bride's family. It occurs only a few times in the Old Testament. Saul replaces the normal payment with a deadly test, hoping it will cost David his life.

christ: The chapter's refrain, that the LORD was with David, points ahead to the promise of 2 Samuel 7 that God would be with David's line and establish a king forever, a promise the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus. There is also a thematic resonance, not a prediction, in the picture of a beloved one whose success stirs the jealousy of those in power, who plot his death in secret while he answers with humility. The Gospels note that the leaders handed Jesus over out of envy (Mark 15:10). Jonathan's self-giving love, handing over his own robe and prospects to the one God had chosen, also shows the kind of love that the New Testament describes in its fullness in Christ, who gave up his own glory for others (Philippians 2:5-8).

hard.q: What kind of love did Jonathan have for David?
hard.a: The chapter says Jonathan loved David "as himself," and some modern readers ask whether the relationship was romantic or sexual. The long-standing Jewish and Christian reading, held by most commentators, sees a deep friendship and covenant loyalty, pointing out that the vocabulary of love and covenant here is also the vocabulary of political alliance, and that nothing in the text describes a sexual relationship. Some modern interpreters argue that the language and David's lament in 2 Samuel 1:26 suggest a romantic bond. Readers should know both readings exist and should weigh them against the text itself. What the chapter unmistakably shows is covenant love that seeks the other's good at great cost: Jonathan, the heir to the throne, hands his robe and weapons to the man God has chosen instead of him.

questions: Jonathan gave David the symbols of his own position. What would it take for you to rejoice in someone else's calling when it replaces your own hopes?
Saul's jealousy began with a song that ranked him second. What comparisons stir envy in you, and what does that envy tend to grow into?
David answered Saul's offers with humility even while Saul was plotting against him. How do you respond when you suspect someone's kindness is a trap?
